recommendations.rationale: MIR gives well-defined absorption bands and is one of the most informative methods for chemical analysis, and ATR is the contact route for a liquid or soft material. This is a precedent that justifies testing MIR-ATR first; it is not proof that it works on this melt.

solution_options.fusion_note: Fusion level: start from one model per method as the baseline, then low-level fusion of the concatenated spectra with block scaling so that neither method dominates. Same sampling spot: both measurements must look at the same material at the same barrel position, or a combined probe must be used; ATR sees a shallow layer while NIR reflection sees a larger, deeper volume. Synchronisation: the data from both methods must be taken simultaneously and normalised to a common time step before fusion. Per-method calibration: each instrument needs its own calibration and its own diagnostics; a fused model breaks if either block drifts or a probe is changed. Must beat the best single method: validate on held-out runs or batches and drop the extra instrument if the fused model is not better.

chemometrics_note: Both routes need a calibration or classification model built on reference values from the offline assays. NIR bands overlap, which makes chemometrics necessary, and NIR and MIR calibrations are specific to the material: an API grade, polymer or additive change requires re-validation on the new material. Build the model on the trial data and validate it on held-out runs or batches.
realtime_tracking_note: The enquiry is about detection while the melt is processed. Fiber probes allow measurement at the process without sampling, and NIR diode-array instruments record all wavelengths at once, which suits fast processes. The measurement point and the time step still have to be fixed with the customer.
future_direction: If the trial identifies a few informative wavelengths, a compact optical multisensor system or a small spectral fiber sensor could be a later, lower-cost route for this process point.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the melt at the intended port is clear and low-scattering, the geometry changes and O1 would be reconsidered with a transmission or transflection probe. If the API has no usable MIR band at the required level, or if build-up cannot be managed within the cleaning interval, the choice moves to NIR reflection or to the combined option O3. The answers to Q1 to Q5 (required accuracy and detection limit, melt optical state and polymer, interface temperature and cleaning regime, fluorescence, reference quality) decide this.
proposal.next_step: Run a multi-method laboratory trial on representative melt samples at process temperature: MIR-ATR and NIR reflection first, with the existing offline assay as the independent reference, against go/no-go numbers agreed with the customer beforehand.

brief_answer: Test mid-infrared ATR first: the supplied material shows API spectra in hot polymer and in-line NIR/MIR-ATR control of polymer extrusion, so MIR-ATR is the most direct single method, with NIR reflection as the lower-effort comparison if the melt is scattering. Before a probe is chosen we need the required accuracy and detection limit, the melt's optical state, the interface temperature and the cleaning regime. This is a provisional plan, not a validated configuration.
